## Design

### 2026-10-14 – Entry 1 — Designing Orbitrail’s Screw Elevator

**6.5h**

Entry 1 — Designing Orbitrail’s Screw Elevator
October 13–14, 2026

Today I started developing Orbitrail, my mechanical marble run project for Half Life. I decided to build my own design, with a hand-cranked screw elevator as the central mechanism. The plan is to lift marbles, release them individually, and eventually send them through two different tracks before returning them to the bottom. This session focused on turning that idea into the first elevator components in Onshape.

I began with the overall layout. I modeled a circular base and established the elevator’s position using a layout sketch. The screw is 140 mm long and inclined at 60 degrees to the horizontal. Working from a layout helped me keep the shaft, housing, and end supports aligned instead of positioning each component independently.

The next step was creating the screw. I modeled an 8 mm diameter central shaft and generated a seven-turn helix along its length, giving it a 20 mm pitch. Creating the plane for the flight profile took some troubleshooting: my initial approach produced a “cannot determine rotation axis” error. I resolved that by using a Curve point plane at the helix’s starting point.

On that plane, I sketched a rectangular flight profile measuring 9.5 mm radially by 2 mm thick. I positioned it with 0.5 mm of overlap into the shaft so the swept flight would join the core. Sweeping this profile along the helix produced the screw as a single solid.

I then modeled the stationary housing around it, using a 27 mm inside diameter and a 31 mm outside diameter. The nominal screw diameter is 26 mm, leaving an initial radial clearance of 0.5 mm. These clearances are starting values that will need to be checked with printed parts.

One important design question came up while looking at the inclined screw: would a marble actually move upward, or would it roll back down? I created an 8 mm reference sphere and used section views to examine how it fit between the shaft, flight, and housing. I also used temporary Boolean intersection checks to look for overlapping geometry. An initial marble position intersected the screw, so I adjusted its position and checked again.

These checks helped me understand the available space, but they do not prove that the elevator will work while rotating. The marble’s movement, friction, and behavior at the entrance still need physical testing.

After that, I worked on the end supports. I designed separate lower and upper caps with clearance holes for the shaft, sleeves that locate around the housing, and internal stops that establish the housing’s axial position. I extended the shaft through both ends, including an upper extension for the drive gear.

I added mounting tabs to the caps and housing, aligned holes for M3 fasteners, and hollow standoffs between the tabs. The standoffs provide support across the gap so tightening the fasteners does not simply bend the tabs together. I used section views throughout this process to inspect the sleeves, stops, and shaft clearances. Interpreting those sections carefully mattered because surfaces behind the cutting plane could look like material blocking the shaft.

The final part of the session was the gear drive. I added the MrT Spur Gear custom feature to Onshape and created a 24-tooth gear for the screw and an 18-tooth gear for the future hand crank. Both use module 1, a 20-degree pressure angle, and a 5 mm face width. I placed their centers 21 mm apart using a gear layout sketch.

To transmit torque to the screw, I created a flat on the upper shaft extension, forming a D-shaped end. I projected that profile into a sketch on the driven gear, enlarged it with an initial 0.15 mm outward offset, and cut the matching hole through the gear. I also adjusted the smaller gear’s angular position so its teeth sat between those of the larger gear.

By the end of the session, I had modeled the screw, housing, both end caps, mounting features, reference marble, and the initial gear pair. The next steps are to design the crank shaft and its support, resolve axial retention, refine the gear clearances, and develop the marble inlet and outlet. After that, I can connect the elevator to the rest of the track system.

This session turned the concept into a substantial CAD model, while also showing which parts still need testing rather than relying on appearance alone.
